Pinned feature sampling. We artificially pinned the value of a feature to a fixed high number and then sample from the model. We find that the generated text matches the interpretation of the feature.
To understand how the geometry of the dictionary elements correspond to these qualitative clusters, we do a 2-D UMAP on the combined set of feature directions from A/0, A/1, and A/2.

A schematic of feature splitting: as the number of learned sparse features increases, a single dictionary direction splits into several nearby directions spanning the same region, so similar features sit at small angles to one another.
In general though, we see that runs with more learned sparse features tend to be more specific than those with fewer.

At a sufficiently coarse level dictionary learning cannot tell the difference between these, but when we allow it to use more learned sparse features, the features split and refine into a zoo of different P features that fire in different contexts.

Put another way, if the present token is made of digits, the model will predict that the next token is a non-digit base64 token.

If we look at the top dataset examples for each feature, we find that examples for A/1/1544 contain substrings which decode as ASCII, while none of the top activating examples for A/1/2357 or A/1/2364 do:

These two notions of similarity correspond to the correlations of the points in the two scatter plots we used when analyzing individual features earlier. We've reproduced the plots for the Arabic feature below:

Feature vs Neuron Universality: histograms of the activation correlation between each A/1 feature (or A neuron) and its most similar counterpart in the independently trained B run, with features (median 0.72) far more universal than neurons (median 0.46).
In the scatterplot below, we find that this kind of disagreement is widespread.
We find that the attribution similarity correlates quite highly with the activation similarity, meaning that features that were coactive between models were useful at predicting the same tokens.
For example, a base64 feature increases the probability of tokens like Qg and zA – plausible continuations which would continue to activate it.

Let's now consider a two-node system for producing variables in "all caps snake case" (e.g. ARRAY_MAX_VALUE). One node (A/0/207) activates on the all caps text tokens, the other (A/0/358) on underscores:

Thus, we observe two features, one of which fires on either complete characters or the suffix (predicting either a new complete character, or a prefix), while the other only fires on the prefixes and predicts suffixes.
The full system can be seen below:
It's important to note that these features can be quite contextual. There are several features related to IRC transcripts which form a totally different finite state automata like system:
This is a relatively standard legal language, and notably occurs in the file headers for popular open source software licenses, meaning the model likely saw it many times during training.

Moreover, it isn't clear that features need to be one-dimensional objects (encoding only some intensity). In principle, it seems possible to have higher-dimensional "feature manifolds" (see earlier discussion here).

Two schematic alternatives to one-dimensional features: a feature manifold that may be equivalent to a set of correlated features, and a manifold that can be approximated by 1-dimensional features but admits no "correct" set of them.
Despite this, kurtosis shows the neuron basis is still privileged.
Many of the feature density histograms are bimodal. For example, consider the feature density histogram for A/16:

In many preliminary small-scale experiments, the two clusters are often perfectly separable. However, for runs with a large number of autoencoder neurons and a large L1 coefficient these two clusters often overlap.
Along these three dimensions, the high density cluster is clearly separable.

As we increase the number of autoencoder neurons (or “N learned sparse”), we continue to discover not only more features but also rarer features, suggesting that we have not exhausted the features in our one-layer transformer.
